title: EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689): phased application
officialTitle: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
regulator: European Parliament and Council / European Commission (AI Office) / national market surveillance authorities
latestUpdate: The Act's general provisions, including Article 50 transparency duties, penalties and national enforcement structures, have applied since 2 August 2026. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI) pushed Annex III high-risk obligations back to 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded high-risk obligations to 2 August 2028.
summary: The AI Act is a horizontal, risk-based regulation for AI systems placed on the market or used in the EU. Its main elements are prohibited practices, obligations for high-risk systems, transparency duties and rules for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. Obligations fall mainly on providers, with lighter but binding obligations on deployers.
buySideImpact: Most UCITS managers and AIFMs act as deployers of third-party AI rather than providers. Their main live obligations are AI literacy (Art. 4), the bans on prohibited practices (Art. 5) and Article 50 transparency for client-facing chatbots and AI-generated content. Investment-decision and portfolio-construction AI is generally not Annex III high-risk. HR uses such as CV screening and staff performance evaluation, and any consumer creditworthiness scoring, are high-risk and bring deployer duties from 2 December 2027. An asset manager that substantially modifies or rebrands a model can become a provider, so the line between deployer and provider must be managed deliberately.
keyRequirements: Art. 5 prohibitions (e.g. manipulative techniques, social scoring, emotion recognition in the workplace) apply from 2 Feb 2025
Art. 4 AI literacy: as amended by the Omnibus, providers and deployers must take proportionate measures to support staff AI literacy
Art. 50: disclose AI interaction (chatbots); label deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest; applies from 2 Aug 2026
Art. 26 deployer duties for high-risk systems (use per instructions, human oversight, monitoring, log retention, informing workers): from 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III
Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment for certain deployers (e.g. credit scoring, life/health insurance pricing)
Penalties of up to EUR 35m or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices

actions.text: Build and maintain an AI system inventory classifying each use case (prohibited, high-risk, Art. 50 transparency, minimal) and recording the firm's role (provider or deployer)
Evidence the AI literacy programme: role-based training for front office, distribution, operations and the board, with attendance records
Add AI-interaction disclosures to client-facing chatbots and to AI-generated marketing and investor communications
Identify HR and recruitment tools that fall under Annex III and plan deployer controls (human oversight, logs, worker notification) for 2 Dec 2027
Update vendor due diligence and contracts to obtain provider conformity information, instructions for use and incident-notification commitments

title: Digital Omnibus on AI: high-risk deadlines deferred (Reg 2026/1744)
officialTitle: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
regulator: European Parliament and Council / European Commission
latestUpdate: The regulation was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. Before that, Parliament endorsed it on 16 June and the Council adopted it on 29 June 2026, following a provisional trilogue deal on 7 May 2026.
summary: The Commission proposed the AI Omnibus in November 2025 as part of its digital simplification package. As adopted, it sets fixed later dates for high-risk obligations: 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. It also softens the AI literacy duty, gives a short grace period for generative-AI output marking and extends SME-type relief to small mid-caps. It adds a new legal basis for processing special-category data for bias detection, strengthens the AI Office's supervision of GPAI-based systems and creates a new prohibition on AI 'nudifier' and CSAM generation.
buySideImpact: Asset managers now have until December 2027 to bring high-risk HR and credit-type use cases into compliance. This gives time to align with the final harmonised standards and the Commission's high-risk classification guidelines. Article 50 transparency was not deferred, apart from the narrow marking grace period, so client-facing GenAI disclosures are already live. The AI literacy duty is now an obligation of conduct ('take measures'), not of outcome, but documented training is still expected. Financial-sector national competent authorities keep supervision of financial institutions.
keyRequirements: Annex III high-risk obligations deferred to 2 Dec 2027; Annex I to 2 Aug 2028 (fixed dates)
Art. 4 AI literacy recast as a duty to take proportionate measures supporting literacy; no guaranteed individual level required
Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking: grace period to 2 Dec 2026 only for GenAI systems already on the market before 2 Aug 2026
Providers relying on the Art. 6(3) 'not high-risk' exemption must still register, via a simplified procedure
New Art. 4a legal basis to process special-category data for bias detection and correction, under strict safeguards
New prohibition on AI systems generating non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM, applying from 2 Dec 2026

actions.text: Re-baseline the AI Act compliance roadmap to the new dates (2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028) and brief the board on what remains live now (Arts. 4, 5 and 50)
Update AI literacy policies and contract clauses drafted against the old 'ensure a sufficient level' wording
Confirm with GenAI vendors their Art. 50(2) marking implementation ahead of 2 Dec 2026
Assess whether the new bias-detection data basis is relevant for any HR or client-facing models, and document the safeguards

title: GPAI obligations, Code of Practice and Commission GPAI guidelines
officialTitle: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (Transparency, Copyright, Safety and Security chapters) and Commission Guidelines on the scope of obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models under the AI Act
latestUpdate: The AI Office's enforcement powers over GPAI providers became exercisable on 2 August 2026. They include information requests, model evaluations, corrective measures and fines of up to 3% of global turnover. Most major US and EU model providers have signed the Code in full. xAI signed only the safety chapter and Meta declined to sign.
summary: GPAI model obligations under Arts. 53 and 55 have applied since 2 August 2025. They cover technical documentation, information for downstream providers, a copyright policy and a public training-data summary, plus extra safety and security duties for systemic-risk models. The Commission published the voluntary Code of Practice on 10 July 2025 and found it adequate in August 2025. It also published GPAI scope guidelines (18 July 2025) and a training-data summary template.
buySideImpact: These obligations bind the LLM vendors whose models asset managers use in research assistants, client communications and coding tools, not the asset managers themselves. Code signatory status and the downstream documentation required under Art. 53 make useful inputs to vendor due diligence on model limitations, copyright and data provenance. If a firm fine-tunes a GPAI model heavily, it may become a GPAI provider, which needs to be checked against the guidelines' compute thresholds.
keyRequirements: Providers must maintain technical documentation and give downstream deployers and providers information on model capabilities and limitations
Copyright compliance policy, including respect for text-and-data-mining opt-outs, and a public training-content summary
Systemic-risk models: model evaluation, adversarial testing, serious-incident reporting and cybersecurity
Models placed on the market before 2 Aug 2025 must comply by 2 Aug 2027
Fines for GPAI providers of up to EUR 15m or 3% of turnover (Art. 101), enforceable from 2 Aug 2026

title: Commission guidelines on prohibited AI practices and AI system definition
officialTitle: Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (C(2025) 884) and Commission Guidelines on the definition of an artificial intelligence system
latestUpdate: Both sets of guidelines remain the Commission's reference interpretation and have not been formally revised. The Omnibus added a new prohibition on 'nudifier' and CSAM systems, applying from 2 December 2026, which these guidelines do not yet cover.
summary: The prohibited-practices guidelines (4 February 2025) explain the Art. 5 bans with examples, covering harmful manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, emotion recognition in the workplace and untargeted facial scraping. The AI-system definition guidelines (6 February 2025) explain the Art. 3(1) definition and indicate that simpler rule-based and traditional statistical systems may fall outside scope. Both are non-binding.
buySideImpact: The definition guidelines help asset managers scope the AI inventory and exclude conventional quant models, such as linear optimisation and basic statistical models, that do not infer outputs autonomously. Distribution teams should check that digital sales journeys and nudging tools do not stray into manipulative or vulnerability-exploiting techniques. HR teams should confirm that no workplace emotion-recognition tools are used, for example in call-centre or interview analytics.
keyRequirements: No AI using subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm
No exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or socio-economic situation
No emotion recognition in the workplace (except for medical or safety reasons)
Use the seven-element AI system definition to scope the inventory (machine-based, autonomy, adaptiveness, inference, etc.)

title: Draft Commission guidelines on high-risk AI classification (Art. 6)
officialTitle: Draft Commission Guidelines on the classification of high-risk AI systems under Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
latestUpdate: The draft guidelines were published on 19 May 2026, and the consultation, extended once, closed on 23 July 2026. Final guidelines had not been confirmed as adopted as of early October 2026.
summary: The draft guidelines give practical examples for classifying systems as high-risk under Annex I and Annex III. They also explain the Art. 6(3) derogation for systems that do not materially influence decisions. For financial services, they treat creditworthiness evaluation and credit scoring of natural persons as high-risk, while a fraud-detection carve-out applies only where fraud detection is the main intended purpose. AML/CFT systems generally fall outside Annex III unless linked to credit decisions.
buySideImpact: The draft confirms that most core asset-management AI, such as research, portfolio construction, trading and operations, is not Annex III high-risk. Exposure is concentrated in HR tools and any consumer-lending or insurance-pricing activities within a wider group. A system that 'materially influences' a decision about an individual can be high-risk even if a human signs off, so the human-in-the-loop design of HR and client-onboarding tools needs care. A provider's generic disclaimer does not override marketing that promotes high-risk uses.
keyRequirements: Classification is driven by the provider's stated intended purpose, assessed against Annex III use-case descriptions
Art. 6(3) derogation applies only to narrow, preparatory or pattern-detection tasks that do not materially influence outcomes; profiling of natural persons is always high-risk
Credit scoring/creditworthiness of natural persons is high-risk; fraud detection is excluded only where it is the main purpose
Employment uses (recruitment, promotion, task allocation, performance monitoring) are high-risk
Providers relying on Art. 6(3) must document the assessment and register the system (simplified procedure)

title: AI Act Art. 50 transparency: Code of Practice and guidelines
officialTitle: Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content (marking and labelling) and Commission Guidelines on transparency obligations under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
regulator: European Commission / EU AI Office / AI Board
latestUpdate: The final Code was published on 10 June 2026 and assessed as adequate by the Commission (8 July) and the AI Board (9 July). The Commission adopted Art. 50 guidelines on 20 July 2026. Art. 50 obligations have applied since 2 August 2026, with a grace period to 2 December 2026 for marking by legacy GenAI systems.
summary: Article 50 requires providers to design AI systems that interact with people so that users know they are dealing with AI, and to mark synthetic content in a machine-readable way. Deployers must disclose deepfakes and AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it has had human editorial review. The voluntary Code and the guidelines set out how to comply, including multi-layer marking and common EU icons.
buySideImpact: Client-facing chatbots on fund websites and investor portals must make clear that users are interacting with AI. AI-generated video or avatars used in marketing, such as synthetic presenters in fund promotions, must be labelled as deepfakes. AI-drafted market commentary published to the public may need labelling unless it goes through documented human editorial review. These duties sit alongside UCITS/AIFMD and MiFID requirements that marketing communications be fair, clear and not misleading.
keyRequirements: Inform natural persons when they interact with an AI system unless obvious from context (Art. 50(1))
Providers mark synthetic audio, image, video and text outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format (Art. 50(2))
Deployers disclose deepfakes (Art. 50(4))
Deployers disclose AI-generated text published on matters of public interest unless subject to human review and editorial responsibility
Information must be given clearly at the latest at first interaction or exposure, and be accessible

title: ESMA public statement on AI in investment services (MiFID II)
officialTitle: ESMA Public Statement on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the provision of retail investment services (ESMA35-335435667-5924)
latestUpdate: The statement remains ESMA's core conduct expectation for AI in investment services. On 26 February 2026 ESMA added a supervisory briefing on algorithmic trading under MiFID II that covers AI governance, testing and outsourcing in algo workflows.
summary: ESMA's statement reminds firms using AI that existing MiFID II obligations apply in full: organisational requirements, conduct of business and acting in clients' best interests. It sets expectations on management-body accountability, transparency to clients about AI use, data quality, testing, monitoring and staff training, and it covers third-party AI tools. ESMA and NCAs said they would continue to monitor AI use and consider further action.
buySideImpact: The statement applies directly to MiFID investment firms and to UCITS ManCos and AIFMs with MiFID top-up permissions (discretionary portfolio management, investment advice). NCAs also use it as a benchmark for collective portfolio management. Firms using AI in portfolio management, suitability, advice or client communications need documented governance and must disclose to clients how AI is used. Management bodies stay accountable for AI-driven decisions, including those made with third-party tools.

title: ESMA sets AI as Union Strategic Supervisory Priority from 2027
officialTitle: ESMA Union Strategic Supervisory Priority on Digital Innovation (initial focus: artificial intelligence and tokenisation)
latestUpdate: On 23 September 2026 ESMA announced a new Union Strategic Supervisory Priority (USSP) on digital innovation from 2027, initially focused on AI and tokenisation. It follows ESMA's 2025 survey of AI use: of 728 respondents, including 277 investment managers, 395 reported 847 use cases, mostly internal and low-autonomy.
summary: A USSP directs coordinated supervisory work by all EU NCAs on a common theme. Under this one, supervisors will map how firms use or plan to use AI in client-affecting processes beyond the back office and run initial checks on the most affected firms. The risks ESMA flags are biased, unclear or misleading AI outputs, products investors find hard to understand, and concentration on a few third-party providers. The priority runs alongside the existing USSP on cyber and operational resilience, which started in 2025.
buySideImpact: From 2027, EU fund managers and investment firms should expect supervisory questionnaires and thematic reviews from their NCA (e.g. CSSF, CBI, AMF, BaFin) on AI use in investment management, distribution and client communications. Firms need to show that governance produces reliable, client-aligned outcomes and that dependence on third-party AI providers is understood and managed. ESMA's survey found that 53% of investment firms and managers had no AI use cases, so firms with only nascent adoption still need an inventory and policy before supervisors ask.
keyRequirements: Supervisors will collect data on AI use in client-facing and investment processes (expect inventory and governance evidence)
Focus on reliability and bias of AI outputs, client-best-interest alignment and understandable products
Focus on concentration and dependency on a small number of AI/third-party providers

title: DORA: ICT third-party risk and CTPP oversight (AI/cloud vendors)
officialTitle: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA) and the ESAs' designation of critical ICT third-party service providers
regulator: European Parliament and Council / ESAs (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA) / NCAs
latestUpdate: On 18 November 2025 the ESAs designated the first 19 critical ICT third-party providers (CTPPs), including major hyperscale cloud providers. 2026 is the first full cycle of direct ESA oversight. AI model providers are not separately designated, but AI services delivered over designated cloud platforms fall within the oversight perimeter.
summary: DORA has applied since 17 January 2025 to UCITS management companies, AIFMs, investment firms and other financial entities. It sets ICT risk-management, incident-reporting, resilience-testing and ICT third-party risk requirements, including a register of information on all ICT contracts and mandatory contractual provisions. AI tools and APIs supplied by third parties are ICT services under DORA.
buySideImpact: Every AI vendor (LLM APIs, AI-enabled research, trading or compliance tools) must be recorded in the DORA register of information and assessed for whether it supports critical or important functions. Contracts must include DORA Art. 30 clauses (audit, access, incident support, exit), which many off-the-shelf GenAI terms lack. Concentration on one hyperscaler or LLM provider must be assessed and backed by exit strategies.

Pre-contract due diligence and risk assessment; Art. 30 mandatory contractual provisions
Exit strategies and concentration-risk assessment for ICT services supporting critical or important functions
Major ICT-related incident classification and reporting, including AI service outages
ICT risk management framework approved and overseen by the management body

title: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 on GDPR and AI models
officialTitle: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
latestUpdate: The opinion remains the reference position of EU data protection authorities. Separately, the Digital Omnibus GDPR amendments, which would codify a legitimate-interest basis for AI development and operation, were still under negotiation in October 2026 (see eu-digital-omnibus-gdpr-ai).
summary: The EDPB said AI models trained on personal data are not automatically anonymous. Anonymity has to be assessed case by case, and extraction of personal data must be highly unlikely. Legitimate interest can serve as a legal basis for developing and deploying AI models, subject to the three-step test, mitigating measures and data subjects' reasonable expectations. Unlawful processing during development can affect the lawfulness of later deployment.
buySideImpact: Asset managers that deploy third-party models or fine-tune models on client, investor or employee data must check the vendor's GDPR basis and whether the model can be treated as anonymous. Unlawful development by a vendor can taint the deployer's own processing. Investor-data uses such as CRM analytics or personalised communications need a documented legitimate-interest assessment or other legal basis, plus DPIAs where the risk is high.
keyRequirements: Case-by-case anonymity assessment of AI models (resistance to extraction and membership inference)
Three-step legitimate interest test (purpose, necessity, balancing) for AI development and deployment
Mitigating measures: pseudonymisation, data minimisation, enhanced transparency, opt-out mechanisms
Deployers should carry out appropriate assessment of whether the model was developed lawfully

actions.text: Add GDPR lawfulness-of-development and anonymity assurances to AI vendor due diligence

title: Digital Omnibus: proposed GDPR changes for AI training and use
officialTitle: Proposal for a Regulation amending Regulations (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), 2018/1724 and others as regards the simplification of the digital legislative framework (Digital Omnibus)
latestUpdate: As of September 2026, negotiations continue and there is no final deal. The Council compromise text (doc 12535/26) keeps a legitimate-interest route for AI development and operation, with a balancing test. Unlike the AI Omnibus, the data and GDPR strand has not been adopted.
summary: The broader Digital Omnibus proposes GDPR amendments including a new provision (Art. 88c) confirming that legitimate interest can be relied on for developing and operating AI systems and models. It also proposes a narrow exception for residual special-category data in training sets and changes to the definition of personal data. Parliament and Council are still negotiating these through the ordinary legislative procedure.
buySideImpact: If adopted, the changes would give firms greater legal certainty for using investor and employee data to fine-tune or operate AI tools, subject to safeguards and an unconditional right to object. Until adoption, firms should continue to rely on EDPB Opinion 28/2024 and existing GDPR practice, and should not build processes that assume the new legal basis.

Proposed: right to object and respect for technical opt-out signals

title: AI Liability Directive proposal withdrawn
officialTitle: Proposal for a Directive on adapting non-contractual civil liability rules to artificial intelligence (AI Liability Directive), COM(2022) 496
latestUpdate: The Commission announced the withdrawal in its 2025 work programme on 11 February 2025, citing no foreseeable agreement. The withdrawal notice was published in the Official Journal on 6 October 2025. The Commission has said it will consider whether a new proposal or another approach is needed.
summary: The AI Liability Directive would have eased claimants' burden of proof for harm caused by AI systems through disclosure obligations and rebuttable presumptions of causality. It has been formally withdrawn. AI-related liability now rests on national tort law, contract and the revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, which covers software including AI and applies to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026.
buySideImpact: No AI-specific civil liability regime will apply to asset managers. Exposure to investors for AI-driven errors stays governed by contract, fund documents, national law and regulatory redress. Contractual allocation of liability with AI vendors, through warranties, indemnities and limits of liability, is therefore the main protection.
keyRequirements: No new obligations; proposal withdrawn
Revised Product Liability Directive covers software/AI as a 'product' (transposition by 9 Dec 2026)
Liability for AI-driven harm continues under national tort and contract law

title: FCA approach to AI: no AI-specific rules; Consumer Duty and SM&CR
officialTitle: FCA AI Update (April 2024) and FCA approach to artificial intelligence in financial services, including AI Input Zone and planned good and poor practice publication
latestUpdate: The FCA has repeated that it will not introduce AI-specific rules and will rely on the Consumer Duty, SM&CR and operational resilience rules. In May 2026 it reopened its AI Input Zone (closed 19 June 2026) to inform examples of good and poor AI practice it says it will publish later in 2026. As of early October 2026, that publication had not been confirmed.
summary: The FCA regulates AI through its existing technology-neutral framework, mapped to the government's five AI principles in its April 2024 AI Update. This covers the Principles for Businesses, Consumer Duty, SM&CR, SYSC governance and outsourcing rules, and operational resilience. Senior managers remain accountable for AI used in their business areas, and the FCA decided against a dedicated AI prescribed responsibility. Further practical guidance has been promised through good and poor practice examples.
buySideImpact: UK asset managers must be able to show which senior manager owns each material AI use case. AI-assisted communications, fund value assessments and client servicing must meet Consumer Duty outcomes, including consumer understanding and avoiding foreseeable harm. Explainability limits and third-party model use do not reduce accountability. Supervisors are likely to test AI governance through Consumer Duty reviews and SM&CR responsibilities maps.
